title: Potential Energy
summary: Potential energy is stored energy waiting to fall, stretch, or spring into action — a ball held high, a stretched rubber band, a raised hammer. Gravity and height decide it: PE = mass × g × height. Lift the block in this model and watch the stored energy rise; release it and watch the energy turn into motion.

plainLanguageExplanation: Potential energy is energy that is stored up and waiting. A block high on a shelf has it because gravity could pull it down; a stretched rubber band has it because it can snap back. The recipe for the height kind is simple: PE (joules) = mass × gravity × height, where gravity on Earth is about 10 N/kg. That's why the higher an object rests and the heavier it is, the more energy hides inside it — dump trucks at the top of a dam hold the city's lights in energy form. This model is a block on a shelf with a lift button and a meter: raise the shelf, the meter climbs; ounce of height in, joule of stored energy out. Release the block and stored potential turns straight into kinetic energy as it falls — the energy doesn't disappear, it just changes job. This is the same stored treasure behind waterfalls, roller coasters, and every toy kettle hawker pulled high.

keyFacts.label: Height formula
keyFacts.value: PE = mass × g × height (g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth)

keyFacts.label: Two heroes
keyFacts.value: More mass or more height both add stored energy

keyFacts.label: Other kinds
keyFacts.value: Stretched springs and rubber bands store elastic potential energy too

whyItMatters: Potential energy is the world's giant battery: hydroelectric dams stored river height, boulders hold danger until they fall, and springs power everything from mousetraps to catapults. Athletes store it in their leg muscles, archers in drawn bows. Understand PE and you understand the way that energy is hidden, saved, and later spent — the engine behind dams, roller coasters, and trampolines.
didYouKnow: Two 1 kg bricks: one on the floor, one on a 10 m shelf. The top brick holds roughly 100 J of stored energy — enough to raise a bit 0.1°C, or to drop it with the crack of a hammer. Raise it twice as high and the stored energy doubles.
